title: Gibson v. Cranage
summary: A buyer who had expressly reserved personal satisfaction with a portrait of his deceased daughter was not required to pay merely because others might regard the portrait as excellent.
notes:
The notes connect Gibson to Mattei, commercial satisfaction, third-party certificates, and forfeiture. They do not establish a general permission to invoke satisfaction dishonestly.

Citation and rule: Gibson v. Cranage, 39 Mich. 49 (1878); where parties agree that payment depends on the buyer's personal satisfaction and the agreement is neither fraudulent nor against public policy, the court will hold them to it, so the buyer's honest dissatisfaction defeats the price claim.

sections.Parties: Gibson solicited the order for an enlarged portrait and sought its price. Cranage was the father whose deceased daughter was depicted.
sections.Material Facts:
Gibson proposed an enlarged picture made from a smaller photograph. Cranage initially objected to ordering it. According to his testimony, Gibson assured him that he need neither take nor pay for the picture unless it was perfectly satisfactory to him in every particular. Gibson’s account likewise made a picture that Cranage would like and recognize the basis for payment.

Cranage disliked the finished picture. Gibson could not obtain a clear explanation of the objection and sent the picture back to the artist for changes. The next day Cranage wrote that it was unsatisfactory, declined another similar picture, and countermanded the order. He refused to inspect the altered picture until the trial, when he found that his objections remained.
sections.Procedural History: Gibson brought an action for the contract price. Judgment favored Cranage. The Michigan Supreme Court affirmed, concluding that the jury charge was as favorable to Gibson as the agreement warranted.
sections.Issue: Was the satisfaction requirement met by an objectively good portrait even though Cranage remained personally dissatisfied?
sections.Holding: No. Under this agreement Cranage’s own satisfaction was the relevant condition, and Gibson had not established its occurrence.
sections.Reasoning:
A portrait of a deceased child involves an intensely personal judgment that an artist or other observer cannot supply for the customer. Cranage might be unable to articulate precisely what was wrong while still finding the picture unacceptable. The court therefore enforced the satisfaction arrangement as made.

The decision did not rest on fraud, mistake, or public policy invalidating the agreement. It also did not decide a dispute over fabricated dissatisfaction. The accompanying questions about refusing to look, painting a barn, and acting in good faith expose limits and comparisons that should remain distinct from the court’s actual factual ruling.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: This is the performance-stage counterpart to Mattei: a satisfaction provision can preserve a genuine choice while the nature of the promised result determines how that choice is judged.

topics.discretion: The customer’s personal judgment controlled satisfaction with a portrait of his daughter.
topics.conditions: Personal satisfaction was the event on which payment depended.
topics.satisfaction: Aesthetic and personal judgment explains the subjective standard.
topics.interpretation: The court read the express assurance in the context of the particular product.
topics.forfeiture: The supplier could receive no contract price despite having arranged the production of a picture.
topics.express-conditions: Cranage's personal satisfaction was an express condition of his duty to pay, and the case shows that an honest-dissatisfaction condition is enforced as written even though it leaves the seller unpaid.
topics.good-faith: A personal-satisfaction condition is policed only by the requirement that the dissatisfaction be honest, which is the good-faith limit exam answers must state.

mnemonic.rationale: A portrait the buyer did not like
